items.definition: A percentage added to the bill for service, usually 10 % or 15 %. When it is included, tipping again is not expected.
items.example: The service charge is already on the bill, so we will just round it up.

items.definition: A small piece of useful advice.
items.example: A tip callout uses the green primary container.

items.definition: Food bought from a stall or a small kitchen at the roadside. It is usually cheap, quick and freshly cooked, but the hygiene is worth watching.
items.example: Let us get something from a street stall near the station instead of waiting for a table.

items.definition: The official office of your country in another country. It issues your passport and provides consular help.
items.example: The embassy gave me an emergency document the same morning.

items.definition: A smaller embassy office in a city other than the capital, serving a region. It does the same passport work.
items.example: There is no embassy here, only a consulate, and it opens at nine.

items.definition: A short-validity passport issued so you can return home, often same day. It normally allows one or two journeys.
items.example: The emergency travel document is valid for this flight and one return.

items.definition: The written record the local police make about a loss or theft. Most embassies require one before issuing any document.
items.example: Here is my police report; the reference number is on the first page.

items.definition: The official declaration that a document has been lost. It is what cancels the old document in the issuing country's records.
items.example: I have already filed the loss report for my passport.

items.definition: The general help your embassy gives to its own citizens abroad, including lost documents, medical emergencies and legal problems.
items.example: They put me in contact with consular assistance straight away.

items.definition: A new full passport issued after the old one is reported lost. It takes longer than an emergency document but works normally.
items.example: The replacement passport will be ready in five working days.

items.definition: A policy that covers things like medical care, cancellation, lost documents and the cost of an emergency replacement passport.
items.example: My travel insurance covers the emergency document and two extra hotel nights.

items.definition: A set of photocopies or photographs of your identity documents, kept apart from the originals, so they can be replaced quickly.
items.example: I keep a copy of my passport at home and one in my email.

items.definition: The first number of a negotiation, which every later number is measured against.
items.example: The seller opened at 120,000, and every figure after that was measured against it.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that claims the supply is limited, so that waiting looks like a loss.
items.example: The scarcity was easy to check: the shelf held six, not two.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that shortens the time available for checking and deciding.
items.example: The urgency was built to stop a phone call: sign tonight or the price changes.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that presents the decisions of other people as evidence for your own.
items.example: The offer came with social proof: nine out of ten customers chose the larger plan.

items.definition: The pressure to return a favour that the other side has given you.
items.example: The discount was the favour, and the renewal at the same price was the bill.

items.definition: The pull of a person you like, used to move the decision away from the terms.
items.example: The liking did not change the price, but it changed who got the last word.

items.definition: The pressure to act in line with what you have already agreed or done.
items.example: He had approved the budget, so the second approval came easier.

items.definition: The weight a loss carries compared with a gain of the same size.
items.example: The same 20,000 hurt as a loss and helped as a saving.

items.definition: The choice of words around a fact, which changes how the fact feels.
items.example: The framing changed nothing: 400 a month is the same money as 4,800 a year.

items.definition: A small, easy agreement that is used later as the reason for a much larger one.
items.example: The free trial was the foot in the door: the yearly contract came next.

items.definition: A large request made first, so that the smaller request looks reasonable.
items.example: The full package at 200,000 was the door in the face, and the single machine was the real order.

items.definition: The best deal you can make if the deal in front of you does not happen.
items.example: Before the meeting he wrote down his BATNA: the other supplier, the price and the date.

items.definition: The price above which the deal is worse than your best alternative.
items.example: He set his walk-away price the week before, and he did not move it in the room.

items.definition: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, and which is used as a reason to continue.
items.example: The sunk cost of the training was the argument for staying in the job.

items.definition: A recipient added to an email and shown to everyone, so all readers can see who else has it.
items.example: I have copied your manager so that she knows the new date.

items.definition: A hidden recipient. The other recipients cannot see that this person has been included.
items.example: I put the whole branch on BCC so nobody sees the full list.

items.definition: A file sent together with the email. It should be named clearly and referred to in the body.
items.example: Please find the attachment, called Quotation-March-2026.pdf.

items.definition: A task that a named person has agreed to do. In longer emails these are listed explicitly.
items.example: There are two action items: sending the figures and confirming the date.

items.definition: A message sent after an earlier one, either to remind someone or to ask for a decision.
items.example: This is a short follow-up to my email of last Tuesday.

items.definition: Taking a matter to a more senior person because it has not moved. Use it only when it is genuinely warranted.
items.example: If we do not hear back by Friday, we will need to escalate this.

items.definition: How long a reply is expected to take. Often agreed in advance rather than assumed.
items.example: Our usual turnaround time for quotations is two working days.

items.definition: The automatic reply sent while you are away, telling people when you will return and who to contact instead.
items.example: You will get an out of office message until 20 April.

items.definition: To send a document to a group of people for information, usually with no action required.
items.example: I circulated the minutes to everyone on the project.

items.definition: The closing line of an email, such as "Kind regards", followed by your name.
items.example: Use a plain sign-off: Kind regards, then your name and title.

items.definition: A temporary fix that makes a problem go away without solving it.
items.example: We applied a band-aid to the payment process, but the real fix is in the accounting system.

items.definition: A way of working around a problem instead of fixing its cause.
items.example: The manual workaround is for us to check the total by hand every Friday.

items.definition: To return to a topic later. Often used to postpone a decision.
items.example: Let us circle back to the budget question after lunch.

items.definition: To have a short conversation with someone about something.
items.example: Can we touch base on Thursday for fifteen minutes?
